lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- Leading Without Shouting
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mirela Lapera | Lesson 9 -- Leading Without Shouting
lesson.grammar_point: modals of advice and obligation: should / shouldn’t (advice), have to / must (obligation), don’t have to (not necessary) x mustn’t (not allowed)

listenings.text: I've been coaching new managers for fifteen years, and I always give them three pieces of advice. First, you should ask more questions and give fewer orders. People support the decisions they help to make. Second, feedback should be specific, and it should happen often. Not once a year, in a formal meeting, but every week, in small doses. And third, and this one surprises people: you don't have to have all the answers. Saying I don't know, let's find out together, makes you more approachable, not less. Your team doesn't need a hero. It needs a leader they can trust.

In my first year as a manager, I made every mistake possible. The biggest one? I tried to do everything myself. I didn't delegate, because I thought it was faster to do the work alone. I was working until midnight, and my team felt I didn't trust them. Morale was very low, and two good people left. It was a hard lesson. Now I do it differently. I have a one-on-one with each person every week, I set expectations at the start of each project, and then I step back and let them take ownership. I still have to make difficult decisions, but I don't have to do everything.

Our company has offices in five countries, and most of my team works from home. The hardest part is knowing how people really feel. You can't see them in the corridor every day. So we have some simple rules. Every meeting must have a clear goal. If it doesn't, nobody has to join it. Managers should call each person for a short chat every week, just to talk, not about deadlines. And one more rule, maybe the most important: managers mustn't send messages to the team late at night or on weekends. If you want people to be team players, you have to respect their time.
